title: New community heritage grant program established
subtitle: Business improvement area board appointments, Seniors' Centre advisory board, county budget update and upcoming notices of motion
overview: Council adopted a Community Heritage Grant Program to help owners of designated heritage properties pay for conservation work. Matching grants would cover up to half of a project, to a maximum of $10,000, with one project per year per property. Planning staff will administer the program, and an existing heritage sub-committee will review applications and make recommendations {{vote:m2}}. The enabling by-law was passed with the other by-laws {{vote:m3}}.
Council also approved, as a consent item, appointments to the Fergus and Elora Business Improvement Area boards of management and the Victoria Park Seniors' Centre Advisory Board {{vote:m1}}.

The Mayor reported that the County of Wellington budget process is underway, with the current rate increase at 4.5%, and that approval is hoped for at the end of the month. Three notices of motion will be considered on January 29, 2024. Council met in closed session, and the Mayor reported no matters arising from it. Funds for the grant program will be confirmed through the annual budget, and staff will report back each year on uptake.

decisions.detail: Council approved a matching grant program for owners of designated heritage properties and delegated its administration to the Managing Director of Planning and Development.
Council passed By-law 2024-01 establishing the Community Heritage Grant Program and By-law 2024-02 appointing the Fergus and Elora Business Improvement Area boards.
Council confirmed members of the Fergus and Elora Business Improvement Area boards of management, with a by-law to reflect the new executives.
Council confirmed seven appointments to the 2024 Victoria Park Seniors' Centre Advisory Board.

debate: Staff said a grant program is the most effective heritage incentive available. It gives owners direct funds and is simpler to run than a tax rebate program, which would need a heritage easement and heavy administration for a small return to owners.

Councillors asked how owners learn about designation. Staff said roughly 1,100 properties are listed but only 115 are designated, and limited resources have prevented more designations. Staff hope the grant will encourage owners to come forward.

Council raised concern that, under provincial changes, listed properties must come off the municipal register by January 1 of next year and cannot be re-added for five years. Staff said those properties would lose the 60-day demolition review. Staff said they know of no municipal power to go beyond the Heritage Act, though an informal list can be kept.

Councillors asked how the grant interacts with other funding and with materials. Staff said it can be combined with Community Improvement Plan grants if the project scope differs. Synthetic materials would be judged case by case against heritage attributes and national conservation standards.

Council asked when staff would report back. Finance staff said the funding allocation policy would likely come to a pre-budget meeting in September or October, and a program report could be timed to match.
